# Discussion

The present study examined whether a bidimensional conceptualization of digital self-efficacy (DSE), distinguishing between General and Specialized DSE, can be identified and meaningfully compared within two major international large-scale assessments, ICILS 2023 and PISA 2022. Overall, the findings support the feasibility of recovering a comparable two-factor structure in both datasets, indicating that students’ perceived capability to perform routine digital tasks is empirically distinct from their perceived capability in more specialized activities (supporting $H_1$). Although achieving this comparability required targeted model refinements in both studies, the observed patterns of misfit offer substantive insights into how adolescents interpret and classify digital tasks in contemporary digital environments.

A first contribution of the study concerns measurement validity and model specification. In both ICILS and PISA, a small set of items exhibited evidence of cross-loadings and local dependence, suggesting that certain digital tasks do not map neatly onto a purely complexity-based distinction between general versus specialized activities. In particular, tasks involving information, communication, and content creation showed consistent empirical overlap, pointing to a component that blurs the boundaries between the two dimensions. For instance, while in previous assessment cycles web page development was considered a distinctive skill of specialized technology users [@fraillon_icils_2015], the present results indicate that it now shares substantial variance with the latent construct of General DSE. These findings do not contradict the bidimensional structure itself; rather, they suggest that the interpretation of what constitutes “specialized” digital engagement may be shifting over time. This shift has important implications for the temporal stability of DSE operationalizations in large-scale assessments.

The observed patterns are consistent with recent developments in digital studies. The diffusion of user-friendly platforms for website building and online publishing has reduced the technical barriers associated with activities that historically required specialized knowledge [@jagtap_no_2024; @lively_integrating_2023]. At the same time, rising standards for sophisticated multimedia production, potentially intensified by social media dynamics and AI-supported content generation, may alter students’ perceptions of difficulty for tasks previously classified as general digital competence [@gardan_usergenerated_2022; @alnaser_impact_2024]. Together, these contextual shifts provide a plausible explanation for why certain tasks migrate across the boundary between General and Specialized DSE, underscoring the need for DSE measurement frameworks to remain responsive to technological change.

The findings also contribute to an ongoing conceptual debate regarding the dimensionality of DSE. Recent proposals advocate for multidimensional DSE measures aligned with competence frameworks such as DigComp [@europeancommissionjointresearchcentre_digcomp_2022; @ulfert-blank_assessing_2022], which organizes digital competence into domains including information and data literacy, communication and collaboration, content creation, safety, and problem solving. While this approach offers a theoretically rich alternative to complexity-based distinctions, the item batteries available in ICILS and PISA are currently too limited to support a psychometrically stable five-dimensional model, and large-scale validation remains scarce. Within these constraints, the present study provides a parsimonious and empirically supported bidimensional solution that is feasible with existing ILSA data and enables systematic comparisons across assessments.

Turning to comparability across groups, invariance results differed across assessments. In PISA, the bidimensional model achieved configural, metric, and scalar invariance across countries, providing strong evidence that the construct is comparable across participating education systems (supporting $H_2$). In ICILS, the model reached configural and metric invariance but failed to meet scalar invariance criteria across countries, indicating that cross-country mean differences should be interpreted with caution and underscoring the importance of explicitly testing between-country comparability before drawing substantive conclusions (partial support for $H_2$). These results reinforce previous evidence of bi-dimensionality on PISA [@hristov_understanding_2026], and suggest that even when a common two-dimensional structure is recoverable, the degree of cross-national comparability may depend on assessment-specific design features and item functioning.

In contrast, gender invariance results were consistently supportive across both assessments. Scalar invariance was established for gender in both ICILS and PISA, indicating that General and Specialized DSE can be meaningfully compared between girls and boys within each dataset (supporting $H_3$). This finding strengthens the validity of gender comparisons in DSE research and suggests that observed gender gaps are unlikely to be artefacts of measurement non-equivalence, at least within the tested frameworks.

Beyond measurement considerations, the descriptive patterns provide substantive insights into digital inequality. Across countries and in both studies, students reported higher levels of General DSE than Specialized DSE, consistent with the notion that routine digital activities are more widely internalized than specialized or computational competencies. Gender differences, consistenly with previous findings [@gebhardt_gender_2019], were clearly dimension-specific: girls tended to report slightly higher General DSE, whereas boys consistently reported substantially higher Specialized DSE across most education systems. This pattern indicates that gender disparities in digital self-efficacy depend critically on the type of digital task domain being assessed (supporting $H_4$).

At the country level, the magnitude of gender gaps in Specialized DSE varied considerably across education systems, and in some contexts these gaps were minimal. This variability suggests that gender differentiation in specialized DSE is context-dependent rather than universal, supporting $H_4$ from a cross-national perspective. In addition, exploratory country-level distributions revealed that higher levels of Specialized DSE and smaller specialized gender gaps were not necessarily concentrated in highly digitalized contexts. This counterintuitive pattern aligns with prior evidence indicating that digital self-efficacy does not map straightforwardly onto objective performance indicators at the country level [@rozman_students_2025], as well as with findings related to the gender equality paradox, which show that gender gaps in STEM-related attitudes can be larger in more gender-equal societies [@marsh_illusory_2021; @guo_crosscultural_2024].

# Conclusions

In sum, the study provides evidence that a two-dimensional representation of DSE is recoverable in both ICILS and PISA ($H_1$), that cross-national comparability is stronger in PISA than in ICILS (partial support for $H_2$), that gender comparisons are supported in both assessments ($H_3$), and that gender and country differences operate in dimension-specific ways ($H_4$). Together, these findings highlight the importance of explicitly testing measurement assumptions when using ILSA data to interpret digital inequalities and to accumulate evidence across international assessments. Future research should examine whether these results reflect reference group effects, cross-cultural differences in calibration, or variation in exposure to and social valuation of specialized digital pathways.

The article provides future researchers with the opportunity to investigate DSE in both ILSAs using a common measurement strategy, while also pointing to three main limitations of the proposed approach. First, achieving acceptable model fit required the removal of a small number of items from the DSE batteries in both assessments, which may reduce content coverage and limit direct comparability with official reporting. Second, cross-national invariance in ICILS did not reach the most restrictive level, indicating that country-level mean comparisons should be interpreted with caution. Third, the analyses relied on a single cycle from each assessment (PISA 2022 and ICILS 2023), which prevents an evaluation of the temporal stability of the measurement models. Future research should extend this approach across multiple cycles to assess whether the two-dimensional structure remains robust as digital environments evolve. In addition, assessment developers may consider expanding and updating DSE item pools to better capture emerging domains of digital competence in rapidly changing educational contexts.
